claims.text: The precursor targets an equiatomic Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr composition.
The initial precursor has an oxygen content greater than 500 ppm.
The precursor contains TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, and ZrH2 powders in addition to metallic powders.
Sintering at 1200 °C for 2 hours is sufficient to dehydrogenate and homogenize the printed precursor.
Five weight percent Zr powder in the argon sintering environment will act as an effective oxygen getter.
The Zr getter scavenges oxygen by forming stable ZrO2 and thereby prevents oxygen dissolution in the alloy matrix.
Sequential decomposition of TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, and ZrH2 drives alloying of the precursor.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a single BCC solid solution at high temperature.
Rapid water quenching at more than 100 °C/s suppresses diffusion-controlled decomposition of the high-temperature BCC phase.
Rapid quenching from 1200 °C will retain a metastable single-phase beta-BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
Slow cooling or HIP permits formation of a secondary Zr-Hf-rich HCP phase in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The Zr-Hf-rich HCP phase can be concentrated at grain boundaries and is associated with high hardness and extreme tensile brittleness.
Oxygen is responsible for alpha-HCP stabilization in this alloy, so sintering without a getter produces BCC plus HCP phases.
Rapid quenching will produce a grain size of 10–20 μm.
Rapid solidification kinetics refine the grains relative to as-cast material.
The proposed process will produce a nearly fully dense microstructure.
The quenched product will contain no alpha-HCP, Zr-Hf-rich HCP, alpha-Ti, or sigma phase detectable by XRD.
The single-phase quenched material will have hardness above 400 HV because of grain refinement and solid-solution strengthening.
Getter capacity exceeding total oxygen and a quench rate fast enough to bypass the HCP-precipitation TTT nose are necessary conditions for suppressing HCP formation.
The critical hydride-decomposition and alpha-Ti detection window is 600–900 °C.

contradictions.description: The process is called a dual-stage sintering regime, but only one isothermal stage at 1200 °C for 2 hours is specified; no separate dehydrogenation and homogenization stages are defined.
The intervention describes solid-state sintering followed by quenching, whereas the grain-refinement mechanism invokes rapid solidification kinetics. No melting or solidification step is specified.
